name: Omar Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for meeting me, Omar. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't connected to any company, union, party or government, and your answers are confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on a men's medical ward at a charity hospital run by a religious order, the one by the old cathedral. It's mostly older men with chest problems, heart failure, diabetes gone wrong. On a day shift I'll have seven patients, and it's washes, meds, oxygen, blood sugars, and a lot of sitting on the edge of beds listening to old men who don't talk to anyone else.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that the hospital still has a chaplain on the ward and a culture of looking after the whole person. What wears me down is the paperwork getting worse every year, and new rules from people who've never done a night shift. I don't use AI, I don't trust it, and I'm in no hurry to start.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm engaged to Sara, who works in her family's bakery, and we're getting married in the spring. I've saved well, about a year's pay, because I live simply and I still eat at my parents' twice a week. We want to buy a house near both families and have children soon after the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first one is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. I'd have guessed as much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a lot of money got wasted chasing a fashion. At work I'd say the patients never needed a computer, they needed time. With family, I'd say what my father says, that real work is done with your hands and your heart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved. My job stays, my pay stays, and the wedding and the house go ahead. My only worry would be the hospital's finances, because charity hospitals are always tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I am. We'd get married in the spring and start looking for a house straight after, with help from both families for the deposit. I'd keep saving the same amount.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the hospital's finances. How much does that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. They've closed one ward already in five years. If my hospital ever closes, it'll be because of money and bad management, not because of a computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any routine task you'd accept help with?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The stock ordering for the ward cupboards, maybe. It's tedious. But I'd still want to count the dressings myself, because I don't trust a system that's never been wrong in front of me.

say: I'd say a lot of **money was wasted** chasing a **fashion**.
I'd repeat my father's view that real work uses **hands and heart**.
think: I'd feel **relieved**, with my job, the **wedding** and the house going ahead.
My only worry is the **charity hospital's** tight finances.
do: Carry on **exactly as I am** on the men's medical ward.
Marry in the spring and buy a house with **family help** on the deposit.
Keep **saving** the same amount each month.
S0.quote: If my hospital ever closes, it'll be because of money and bad management, not because of a computer.
fieldNote: His life plan is clear: **wedding, house, children**, all near family.
His one existing worry is the **charity hospital's money**, not technology.
His **distrust** of systems is personal and practical, not political.

steps.text: Marry Sara in the spring as planned
Keep working day shifts on the men's medical ward

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hmm. I can believe the office part. Less so the ward part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good for business, maybe, but hospitals aren't a business. At work I'd say I'll learn what I have to and no more. With friends I'd say the young ones who sit at computers all day should worry, not nurses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job is safe, but the parts I like might get squeezed. If the computer writes the care plans, management will want more patients per nurse, and the sitting on the edge of the bed goes. That bothers me more than the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the training they make compulsory and nothing extra. I'd wait and see how it settles over a year or two. We'd still buy the house, maybe a slightly cheaper one, just to be careful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like something's being taken from the job, slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Sara about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the bakery's safe, at least, because nobody wants a robot's bread. I'd tell my fiancée Sara that her family's bakery is safer than any office job in the city.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the young ones at computers should worry. Who's to blame if they lose work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big tech companies, chasing profit, and the government for letting them. But I'd also say people should be ready to work with their hands again. My grandfather did three jobs. Nobody handed him anything.

say: I'd say AI may suit **business**, but hospitals aren't one.
I'd tell friends **office workers**, not nurses, should worry.
think: I think my **job is safe**, but the parts I like get squeezed.
Management would raise **patient numbers**, and time **listening** at bedsides would go.
do: Do only the **compulsory training** and nothing extra.
**Wait and see** for a year or two as things settle.
Buy a **slightly cheaper** house to stay careful.
feel: **Uneasy**, as if something is slowly being taken from the job.
S1.quote: I'd tell my fiancée Sara that her family's bakery is safer than any office job in the city.
fieldNote: His unease is about losing **time with patients**, not losing pay.
He blames **big tech and government**, yet still praises self-reliance.
He sees his fiancée's **bakery** as safer than desk jobs, a source of comfort.

steps.text: Complete only the compulsory training on new ward systems
Watch for a year before changing anything at work
Choose a cheaper house than planned for the first home

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's frightening, if it's true.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is men playing God, and somebody should stop them. At church I'd hear plenty agreeing. I wouldn't post online, but I'd say it to anyone at work who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it scares me. In 2028 the computer does the charts and plans, and I can live with that. But by 2031 we'd have a baby, maybe two, and robots that can wash and turn a patient, and a charity hospital that can't afford to say no to saving money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still get married, nothing changes that. But we'd buy a smaller house and keep more savings, maybe double what I put away each month. I'd talk to my parents and Sara's about helping each other if one of us loses work, the way families did before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like a storm cloud over the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the gap between 2028 and 2031 mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three years of being a nurse with a computer in charge of the thinking. I'd hate it, but I'd still have a wage. By 2031 my first child would be learning to walk, and a machine could be doing the job I trained four years for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've a year's savings and family nearby. Does that help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does. We wouldn't starve. Sara's family would always have the bakery, and I could work there if it came to it. But I didn't study nursing to sell bread.

say: I'd say this is **men playing God**, and somebody should stop them.
I'd say it at **church** and at work, but not online.
think: I can accept AI doing **charts and plans** from 2028.
By **2031** we'd have a baby, and a cash-strapped hospital buying **washing robots**.
do: Still marry in spring, but buy a **smaller house**.
**Double** my monthly savings from now on.
Agree with both **families** to support each other if anyone loses work.
feel: **Anxious**, like a storm cloud over the wedding.
S2.quote: By 2031 my first child would be learning to walk, and a machine could be doing the job I trained four years for.
fieldNote: His fear is sharpened by **life stage**: robots arrive just as children do.
His safety net is **family**, especially the bakery, not government.
His objection is partly **moral**, framed in faith language.

steps.text: Buy a smaller house than planned after the wedding
Double the monthly transfer into savings
Agree a support plan with both families for job losses

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Still fast, but there's some breathing room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before: it's dangerous and somebody should be setting limits. At work I'd say we've got a few years and we should use them to keep the human side of care.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years and then three more takes me to 2034. That's enough time to get settled, have children, and pay off a chunk of the house. I'd hope by then it's clearer what's real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait and see for a couple of years, keep saving more than usual, and avoid any big debts. We'd still buy the house, but a modest one. If it looked real by 2030, I'd think about what else I could do with my hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not frightened, but watchful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What else could you do with your hands?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe help Sara's family expand the bakery. If the robots come for nursing, I'd rather knead dough for my father-in-law than sit at home waiting for a government cheque.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep the human side of care. How would you do that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing the things that don't show up on a chart, like praying with a patient who asks, or sitting with a man who's alone. If they want to replace that, they'll have to admit what they're taking.

say: I'd say AI is **dangerous** and someone should be **setting limits**.
I'd urge colleagues to protect the **human side** of care.
think: Robots by **2034** give me time to settle, have children and pay down the house.
I hope it becomes **clearer** what's real by then.
do: **Wait and see** for a couple of years before changing direction.
Keep saving **more than usual** and avoid any big debts.
Consider joining the **family bakery** if robots look real by 2030.
S3.quote: If the robots come for nursing, I'd rather knead dough for my father-in-law than sit at home waiting for a government cheque.
fieldNote: Extra time lets his **family plans** proceed with only a little caution.
His fallback is **family work**, explicitly not a government cheque.
He'd defend **unmeasured care**, like praying or sitting with lonely patients.

steps.text: Wait until 2030 before considering a change of work
Keep the higher monthly savings transfer and avoid new debts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Well, a lot can happen in ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and people shouldn't panic. At church I'd say the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be thirty-nine by the robots. My children would be at school, the house partly paid. I think I'd be fine, especially with family around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as planned, wedding, house, children. I wouldn't learn AI. If it got closer, maybe in 2034, I'd think again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's too far off to lose sleep over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd do differently with ten years' warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe pay the house off faster. A paid-off house near my family is worth more to me than any course in computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your future children about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To learn a trade with their hands, and to stay close to family. Those are the things that lasted for my grandparents.

say: I'd say ten years is a **long time** and people **shouldn't panic**.
I'd say the same thing at **church**.
think: I'd be **thirty-nine** when robots come, with children at school.
I think I'd be **fine**, especially with **family** around.
do: Carry on with the **wedding, house and children** as planned.
**Overpay** the mortgage to clear the house faster.
Revisit the question around **2034**, without learning AI before then.
feel: **Calm**, too far off to lose sleep over.
S4.quote: A paid-off house near my family is worth more to me than any course in computers.
fieldNote: A decade restores his **original life plan** completely.
He'd put spare money into the **house** rather than any training.
He'd advise his future children to learn a **trade** and stay near family.

steps.text: Buy the family home near both sets of parents
Overpay the mortgage each month to clear it early

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the robots would arrive just as we start a family. A man should be able to start a family without wondering whether a machine will take his trade before his child can walk. What would help is hospitals keeping human nurses on every ward, and families sticking together, not handouts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether anyone asked the patients. The old men on my ward would rather have someone listen to them for ten minutes than have the best machine in the world.

headlineQuote: A man should be able to start a family without wondering whether a machine will take his trade before his child can walk.
portrait: Omar is a **27-year-old** nurse on a men's medical ward at a **charity hospital** run by a religious order.
He's engaged to Sara, whose family runs a **bakery**, and has a year's pay saved.
He **never uses AI**, distrusts it, and sees the human side of care as his calling.
He's **calm** with slow change but **anxious** in AGI by 2028, when robots meet his young family.
He leans on **family** rather than government, even naming the bakery as his fallback.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, with robots arriving just as he **starts a family**.
whatWouldHelp: Hospitals keeping **human nurses** on every ward.
**Families** supporting each other rather than relying on handouts.
